cards.scenario: Enable CloudTrail in all existing and future org accounts; most operationally efficient.
cards.ok: Organizational trail created in the management account.
cards.bad: EventBridge rule plus Lambda that periodically checks and creates trails per account.
cards.why: Org trail auto-covers new member accounts; periodic scripts or manual trails add overhead.

cards.scenario: EC2 in Account B must assume role created in Account A via CloudFormation.
cards.ok: In Account A, role trust policy names Account B's EC2 instance role ARN for AssumeRole.
cards.bad: In Account A, trust policy allows AssumeRole from Account B's root principal.
cards.why: Trust policy of the target role must name the specific EC2 role; root trusts the whole account.

cards.scenario: Find and prevent EC2 launches missing Project tag across org (select three).
cards.ok: SCP denying ec2:RunInstances without tag + Config rule per account + Config aggregator.
cards.bad: IAM policy per account denying ec2:RunInstances + Security Hub as tag aggregator.
cards.why: SCP enforces org-wide centrally; Config rules plus aggregator detect untagged resources.

cards.scenario: Centralized AD-based workforce identities, group/role access across accounts.
cards.ok: IAM Identity Center connected to AD using SAML 2.0, SCIM automatic provisioning.
cards.bad: Cognito user pool linked to AD via SAML 2.0 and SCIM.
cards.why: IAM Identity Center is the workforce SSO for multi-account access; Cognito is for app users.

cards.scenario: Only supervisory roles run IAM actions in all accounts; minimal admin effort.
cards.ok: SCP at root OU denying IAM actions to non-supervisory roles.
cards.bad: IAM permissions boundaries to limit IAM actions to supervisors.
cards.why: SCPs apply org-wide centrally; they attach to OUs or accounts, not individual users.

cards.scenario: Central shared VPC for Customers OU accounts to use but not manage (select two).
cards.ok: Enable RAM sharing with Organizations + RAM share of shared VPC subnets with Customers OU.
cards.bad: SCP on Customers OU denying VPC management actions.
cards.why: Sharing VPC subnets via RAM lets member accounts use the VPC while the owner manages it. SCP alone shares nothing.

cards.scenario: GitHub Actions needs dynamic short-lived AWS credentials replacing IAM user keys; minimal overhead.
cards.ok: IAM OIDC IdP for GitHub; IAM role trusting sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity; pipeline assumes the role.
cards.bad: Amazon Cognito as OIDC IdP with user pool; pipeline authenticates via Cognito to assume role.
cards.why: GitHub is itself an OIDC IdP, so trust it directly in IAM; Cognito adds an unneeded intermediary.

cards.scenario: Auto-deploy VPC CloudFormation template across org, including newly joined accounts (select two).
cards.ok: Management account stack set, service-managed permissions, automatic deployment + StackSets trusted service in Organizations.
cards.bad: Self-managed stack set in member accounts, deployment targets per OU, drift detection for new accounts.
cards.why: Service-managed stack sets with automatic deployment cover new accounts; drift detection does not deploy anything.

cards.scenario: QA members self-launch temporary CloudFormation environments with least privilege.
cards.ok: Service Catalog product of CloudFormation templates with launch constraint; QA group gets Service Catalog APIs.
cards.bad: QA members assume the QA Manager's IAM role, restricted to templates and their resources.
cards.why: Launch constraint provisions with a service role, so QA needs no direct CloudFormation, EC2 or Auto Scaling rights.

cards.scenario: Remote employees reach VPC apps over VPN with MFA.
cards.ok: Client VPN endpoint using AD Connector to directory, MFA enabled on the AD.
cards.bad: Client VPN endpoint with Directory Service via Direct Connect, MFA enabled.
cards.why: Client VPN is for remote users; MFA comes through AD Connector directory integration.

cards.scenario: Add Direct Connect redundancy and reach new VPC in us-west-1 over same network.
cards.ok: Second connection, Direct Connect gateway, private VIFs, virtual private gateway per VPC.
cards.bad: Second connection with private VIFs, one transit gateway per Region's VPC.
cards.why: A Direct Connect gateway spans Regions via private VIFs and VGWs; a private VIF reaches one Region.

cards.scenario: Isolate dev from prod traffic on a shared transit gateway.
cards.ok: Remove default route table association and propagation; separate dev and prod TGW route tables.
cards.bad: Tag each VPC attachment env and write policies restricting traffic between environments.
cards.why: Isolation comes from separate route tables per environment; tags don't control routing.

cards.scenario: Lambda must reach DynamoDB and Neptune in private subnets (select two).
cards.ok: Lambda in private subnets with Neptune SG access + DynamoDB VPC endpoint, or NAT gateway.
cards.bad: Lambda in public subnets routed through the Internet Gateway.
cards.why: Lambda in public subnets gets no public IP, so the internet gateway can't reach DynamoDB.

cards.scenario: Scale virtual appliances horizontally, private cross-account connectivity, minimal manual setup (select two).
cards.ok: ASG with launch template user data + Gateway Load Balancer exposed via PrivateLink endpoint service.
cards.bad: ASG + Application Load Balancer distributing traffic to the appliances.
cards.why: GWLB (layer 3) fronts appliances; GWLB endpoints give private cross-VPC access; ASG automates scaling. ALB is layer 7.

cards.scenario: Expose on-premises services privately to other AWS-hosted e-commerce businesses, data off public internet.
cards.ok: VPC Endpoint Service on a Network Load Balancer (TCP); keep Direct Connect to the data center.
cards.bad: VPC Endpoint Service linked to an Application Load Balancer (HTTP/HTTPS).
cards.why: PrivateLink endpoint services require an NLB (or GWLB) front end; an ALB cannot back an endpoint service.

cards.scenario: Staging account frequently re-provisioned must reconnect to ops account apps; flexible reconfiguration.
cards.ok: Share the transit gateway with staging via AWS RAM; enable automatic acceptance of attachments.
cards.bad: Per-connection new transit gateway in staging; send peering requests to ops account transit gateway.
cards.why: A RAM-shared TGW with auto-accept lets staging attach and detach VPCs freely; per-connection TGWs and peering are heavy.

cards.scenario: On-premises reach VPCs over transit VIF via Direct Connect gateway and transit gateway (select two).
cards.ok: Allowed prefixes same or wider than VPC CIDR + advertise VPC prefix list on DX gateway TGW association.
cards.bad: MACsec must_encrypt on the connection + upgrade 200 Mbps to 500 Mbps.
cards.why: Reachability is controlled by DX gateway allowed prefixes; MACsec and bandwidth do not affect routing.

cards.scenario: Add North American users to CloudFront weather maps; LEAST latency (select two).
cards.ok: Lambda@Edge routes NA requests to new us-east-1 S3 bucket + S3 cross-region replication.
cards.bad: Lambda@Edge routes NA requests to S3 Transfer Acceleration endpoint of existing bucket.
cards.why: Region-local replicated bucket with Lambda@Edge routing gives closest origin; Transfer Acceleration targets uploads.

cards.scenario: Cut latency for Asia and Middle East users, MOST cost-effective (select two).
cards.ok: S3 Transfer Acceleration + switch API Gateway to Edge-Optimized endpoint.
cards.bad: Deploy Lambda and S3 per Region, replication, Route 53 Geolocation routing.
cards.why: Transfer Acceleration and Edge-Optimized API use edge network cheaply; multi-Region duplication costs more.

cards.scenario: Two-Region ALBs: serve nearest Region for speed; fail over to the other if it is down.
cards.ok: Route 53 latency alias records with health checks and Evaluate Target Health on each ALB.
cards.bad: Route 53 geolocation records to nearest ALB with periodic health checks.
cards.why: Latency routing picks lowest-latency healthy Region; geolocation maps by user location, not measured speed.

cards.scenario: Fargate task misconfig causes ALB 502s; show custom error page, least operational overhead.
cards.ok: S3 error page as CloudFront origin (OAC); CloudFront custom error response on 502.
cards.bad: ALB listener rule for /* with fixed-response action returning 502 and custom body.
cards.why: CloudFront custom error responses serve a custom page on origin 502; a catch-all fixed response would block all traffic.

cards.scenario: Idle transcoder EC2, process each file once; HA, scalable, MOST cost-effective, low management.
cards.ok: ECS on Fargate task; Lambda calls RunTask on S3 upload event.
cards.bad: S3 events to SQS, EC2 Auto Scaling group with minimum size of one instance.
cards.why: Fargate runs only per upload with no servers; EC2 minimum-one stays idle and costs.

cards.scenario: Auto-scale app and Aurora tiers for unpredictable traffic spikes (select two).
cards.ok: ALB with ASG, round-robin + Aurora Auto Scaling of read replicas.
cards.bad: NLB ASG with sticky sessions and Least Outstanding Requests algorithm.
cards.why: Aurora Auto Scaling adjusts replicas, not writers; ALB supports sticky sessions with round-robin.

cards.scenario: Mixed Java/Node apps, 2-4 hour jobs; standardize deployment, scale, MOST cost-effective.
cards.ok: Containerize apps as ECS tasks on EC2 cluster with EC2 Auto Scaling.
cards.bad: Containerize to Lambda container images with provisioned concurrency.
cards.why: Long 2-4 hour jobs exceed Lambda limits; ECS on EC2 standardizes and scales on utilization.

cards.scenario: Feature-branch pipeline with unit testing; separate dev and production artifacts.
cards.ok: Separate CodePipeline triggered by feature branch; CodeBuild unit tests, stage artifacts in S3.
cards.bad: Separate CodePipeline with Lambda stage performing unit testing.
cards.why: CodeBuild runs unit tests and builds artifacts; Lambda is not a build service.

cards.scenario: ECS on EC2 with NAT gateway to S3; cut cost without hurting availability (select two).
cards.ok: Scheduled scaling instead of predictive + S3 Gateway VPC endpoint replacing NAT gateway.
cards.bad: Spot Instances capacity provider with even weight + S3 Intelligent-Tiering.
cards.why: Gateway endpoint removes NAT data charges; scheduled scaling suits known peaks. Spot risks availability.

cards.scenario: Containerized app with HA SQL Server, no DB password inside container.
cards.ok: RDS SQL Server Multi-AZ, Secrets Manager secret, Fargate with Service Auto Scaling.
cards.bad: SQL Server on EC2 Auto Scaling group with encrypted Parameter Store credentials.
cards.why: Managed Multi-AZ RDS plus Secrets Manager keeps credentials out of container; Fargate avoids servers.

cards.scenario: Monolithic .NET API on EC2, spiky traffic, unresponsive at peak: cheapest, least ops?
cards.ok: Split into Lambda functions behind API Gateway REST API; custom domain; Route 53 record to it.
cards.bad: Existing EC2 in ASG behind ALB, scale on RequestCountPerTarget; Route 53 to ALB.
cards.why: Serverless pay-per-use scales each function independently; EC2 monolith must scale as a whole unit, costing more.

cards.scenario: Fargate task cannot reach Aurora MySQL; DB_HOST and Secrets Manager DB_PASSWORD (select three).
cards.ok: DB_HOST = cluster endpoint; Aurora SG allows Fargate on 3306; valueFrom = secret ARN.
cards.bad: DB_HOST = instance endpoint; valueFrom = secret name.
cards.why: Cluster endpoint follows failover; valueFrom needs the secret ARN; the DB security group must allow inbound from tasks.

cards.scenario: 15-20 minute framework install in EC2 user data slows deployments; speed it up?
cards.ok: Systems Manager Automation (AWS-CreateImage) builds custom AMI with framework preinstalled; use it as baseline.
cards.bad: Compress framework files in S3; user data script pulls them.
cards.why: A prebaked AMI removes the install step at launch; smaller downloads still run the full install.

cards.scenario: E-commerce browsing and checkout modules load unevenly; JWT sessions; scale each independently, cost-efficient.
cards.ok: Separate ECS services with own auto scaling; CloudFront Functions inspect JWT and route by module.
cards.bad: API Gateway in front of ECS, Lambda authorizer on JWT, route by JWT attributes.
cards.why: Per-module ECS services scale independently; CloudFront Functions inspect JWT cheaply at edge. API Gateway plus authorizer adds cost and layers.

cards.scenario: Single EC2 web app freezes at peak; read-heavy RDS PostgreSQL; improve reliability with minimal development.
cards.ok: EC2 Auto Scaling group behind load balancer; migrate to Aurora with Aurora Replicas for reads.
cards.bad: Auto Scaling group, CloudFront origin, RDS Multi-AZ with standby used for reads.
cards.why: ASG plus ELB removes the single point of failure; Aurora Replicas serve reads, while a Multi-AZ standby cannot serve reads.

cards.scenario: Social webhook service on EC2/ALB to serverless, most operationally efficient.
cards.ok: Lambda with a Lambda Function URL per webhook; platform sends webhook calls to the URLs.
cards.bad: Lambda behind API Gateway REST API, proxy integration, one API resource per webhook.
cards.why: Function URLs expose Lambda over HTTPS directly, without API Gateway to manage.

cards.scenario: Video encoding Lambda times out on longer clips; never again, no infrastructure to manage (select two).
cards.ok: Containerize encoder to ECR image + Fargate ECS task started by Lambda on S3 PUT.
cards.bad: Step Functions Map/Parallel splitting work, Provisioned Concurrency on each Lambda.
cards.why: Fargate tasks have no 15-minute limit and no servers; Lambda steps still time out, provisioned concurrency only pre-warms.

cards.scenario: Event-driven serverless redesign plus future multi-cloud clusters; most efficient.
cards.ok: EKS with Fargate; Aurora Serverless MySQL + Redshift Serverless; EventBridge for data flow.
cards.bad: ECS with Fargate; Aurora Serverless MySQL + Redshift Serverless; EventBridge for data flow.
cards.why: EKS (Kubernetes) is portable across other clouds; ECS is AWS-specific so multi-cloud clusters do not fit.

cards.scenario: RDS MySQL CPU spikes at peak from Lambda; updates lost (select two).
cards.ok: SQS standard queue per Lambda subscribed to SNS + RDS Proxy in front of RDS.
cards.bad: More RDS read replicas + RDS Data API for Lambda.
cards.why: Queues buffer writes and RDS Proxy pools connections; read replicas do not help write load.

cards.scenario: App slowdowns: high Lambda invocations, DB connections, RDS CPU (select two).
cards.ok: ElastiCache for Redis caching hot data + Lambda using RDS Proxy.
cards.bad: RDS Multi-AZ + larger Lambda timeout and concurrency limits.
cards.why: Caching cuts DB reads; RDS Proxy pools connections. Multi-AZ is availability, not performance.

cards.scenario: Convert MP4 training videos to HLS, cost-effective, HA, good quality.
cards.ok: MediaConvert queue transcodes to HLS into S3 with lifecycle management.
cards.bad: Elastic Transcoder pipeline with output hosted on large EBS volumes.
cards.why: MediaConvert is the managed file-based transcoding service producing HLS to S3.

cards.scenario: Lambda to Aurora shows many idle DB connections at high demand (select two).
cards.ok: RDS Proxy with function using proxy endpoint + DB connection initialized outside the handler.
cards.bad: Provisioned Concurrency for the Lambda function.
cards.why: Pooling (RDS Proxy) plus connection reuse across invocations cuts connections; Provisioned Concurrency only removes cold starts.

cards.scenario: Mask PAN, transform records to JSON on S3 delivery; easily expandable transformations?
cards.ok: Glue crawler with custom classifier; Lambda on S3 delivery triggers Glue ETL job outputting JSON to another bucket.
cards.bad: Lambda extracts records to SQS; Fargate scales on queue depth, transforms, writes JSON to S3.
cards.why: Serverless Glue ETL is purpose-built for extensible transforms; custom classifier handles the format. Fargate/SQS means custom code.

cards.scenario: Patient records on Managed Blockchain: private exchange, secure, immutable. Where to store PII?
cards.ok: Lambda stores hash of each PII item on blockchain; PII off-chain in DynamoDB.
cards.bad: Only name and ID on blockchain; other PII off-chain in DynamoDB.
cards.why: Hash on-chain proves integrity and immutability without exposing PII; name and ID on-chain would still expose PII.

cards.scenario: Replace plain port-25 SMTP server with Amazon SES; domain already validated; how to connect?
cards.ok: SES SMTP credentials from console; point app at SES SMTP endpoint; port 587 with STARTTLS.
cards.bad: IAM user access keys used directly against the SES SMTP endpoint on port 587.
cards.why: SMTP endpoint needs SES-derived SMTP credentials, not raw IAM access keys; connections must use TLS.

cards.scenario: SQS-fed EC2 crawlers sit idle at low volume, JSON files on EFS: most cost-effective (select two).
cards.ok: Replace EC2 with Lambda processing the SQS queue + store the JSON files in S3 instead of EFS.
cards.bad: EC2 Spot Instances for the web-crawling process.
cards.why: Lambda bills only when processing; S3 is cheaper than EFS. Spot can be interrupted and still bills idle time.

cards.scenario: Redshift Spectrum queries on VPC flow logs slow; improve performance and cut storage most.
cards.ok: Configure VPC Flow Logs output in Parquet format, partitioned by hour.
cards.bad: Compress flow logs with bzip2 instead of gzip.
cards.why: Columnar Parquet with partitions lets Spectrum skip irrelevant data and read less; swapping compression codec barely helps queries.

cards.scenario: Cut OpenSearch storage cost; slow queries on old data OK; keep full audit copy.
cards.ok: Downsize data nodes, add UltraWarm, ISM to cold after 1 week, S3 lifecycle to Glacier Deep Archive.
cards.bad: Same design but S3 lifecycle moves data older than 3 months to S3 Infrequent Access.
cards.why: Cold tier suits rarely queried data; Deep Archive is the cheapest audit copy. S3 Infrequent Access costs more.

cards.scenario: Assess TCO for on-premises Kubernetes and databases before migrating; best tool?
cards.ok: Migration Evaluator: Collector data imported, export Quick Insights report.
cards.bad: AWS Transform MGN test migration, then generate TCO report.
cards.why: Migration Evaluator (ex-TCO Calculator) estimates cost from collected on-premises data; MGN migrates, not TCO.

cards.scenario: Cross-region DR, RPO under 1 minute, RTO 15 minutes, MOST cost-effective.
cards.ok: CloudFormation, Aurora global database, Elastic Disaster Recovery, ASG, Route 53 failover.
cards.bad: Warm-standby scaled-down replica with one EC2 instance and Aurora instance running.
cards.why: Elastic Disaster Recovery plus Aurora global DB meets tight RPO/RTO without a running warm replica.

cards.scenario: Org-wide S3 usage trends over 6 months across accounts and Regions; least development.
cards.ok: S3 Storage Lens custom organization dashboard with advanced metrics.
cards.bad: S3 Storage Class Analysis visualizations in the S3 console.
cards.why: Storage Lens aggregates org-wide usage and activity trends; Class Analysis is per-bucket tiering.

cards.scenario: Convert Single-AZ FSx to Multi-AZ with minimal downtime.
cards.ok: DataSync copy to new Multi-AZ FSx, then repoint applications.
cards.bad: Backup current FSx and restore to a new Multi-AZ file system.
cards.why: Deployment type cannot be changed in place; DataSync copy to a new Multi-AZ file system.

cards.scenario: Understand usage and dependencies on-premises; right-size EC2 before migrating.
cards.ok: Transform discovery tool, migration planning waves, migration assessments for EC2 right-sizing recommendations.
cards.bad: Transform discovery tool, waves, then Compute Optimizer right-sizing after migration to EC2.
cards.why: Migration assessments right-size before migration; Compute Optimizer only works after workloads already run on EC2.

cards.scenario: Move VMware VMs to EC2 preserving installed software and configuration.
cards.ok: Export VMs as OVF, S3 bucket, VM Import/Export role, CLI import-image.
cards.bad: Systems Manager hybrid activation, then EC2 Image Builder golden AMI.
cards.why: VM Import/Export converts the existing VM image to an AMI, keeping stack intact.

cards.scenario: Replace SFTP server, higher availability, partners keep same connection method.
cards.ok: Transfer Family server in VPC with internet-facing endpoint, S3 bucket, move Elastic IP.
cards.bad: Transfer Family SFTP server with publicly accessible endpoint, Elastic IP disassociated.
cards.why: VPC internet-facing endpoint can reuse the Elastic IP so partners need no change.

cards.scenario: Scale 3 to 50 EC2 web instances, no app changes, shared content, no data loss.
cards.ok: EFS for shared files; move app to Elastic Beanstalk with ALB and Auto Scaling.
cards.bad: EBS Multi-Attach storage with Elastic Beanstalk and Network Load Balancer.
cards.why: EFS provides shared NFS storage across instances; Beanstalk manages the scaling stack. Multi-Attach is not general shared storage.

cards.scenario: DR RTO 30 min, RPO 1 hour for RDS MySQL; Route 53 managed (select two).
cards.ok: Cross-region RDS read replica promoted automatically by Lambda + Route 53 failover record to replica.
cards.bad: Hourly Lambda backup to S3 in secondary Region + Route 53 health checks to standby.
cards.why: Cross-region read replica replicates asynchronously for low RPO, with fast promote and DNS failover for RTO.

cards.scenario: Master satellite data must replicate to secondary bucket within 30 minutes.
cards.ok: Replication rule filtered on master prefix with S3 Replication Time Control enabled.
cards.bad: Separate replication rule for master prefix, relying on standard replication.
cards.why: S3 RTC replicates 99.99% of objects within 15 minutes; standard replication has no SLA.

cards.scenario: Custom SFTP on single EC2 uploading nightly to S3: improve reliability and scalability?
cards.ok: AWS Transfer for SFTP; Route 53 record points to the server endpoint hostname.
cards.bad: NLB TCP listener with ASG of EC2 instances hosting SFTP; Route 53 to NLB.
cards.why: Transfer Family is managed, multi-AZ, auto-scaling, writes straight to S3; self-managed ASG keeps the ops burden.

cards.scenario: Heterogeneous migration SQL Server to managed AWS database, minimal operational overhead.
cards.ok: AWS SCT converts schema SQL Server to MySQL; RDS for MySQL target; AWS DMS migrates data.
cards.bad: Native SQL Server backup to S3, then AWS Glue loads data into RDS MySQL.
cards.why: SCT plus DMS is the standard heterogeneous path; a SQL Server backup cannot restore into MySQL.

cards.scenario: DR for RDS with minimal data loss across Regions, plus offload heavy analyst queries.
cards.ok: Cross-Region RDS read replica for analyst queries; promote at disaster; replicate AMIs; S3 CRR.
cards.bad: Hourly cross-Region RDS snapshots + ElastiCache; restore snapshot and launch from AMIs on disaster.
cards.why: Cross-Region read replica gives near-continuous replication and absorbs analysis; hourly snapshots lose up to an hour of data.

cards.scenario: Migrate on-premises Windows file server data to AWS, available as a file system to Windows servers.
cards.ok: FSx for Windows File Server share; schedule daily DataSync task from on-premises file server to it.
cards.bad: EFS share populated by DataSync and mounted on the Windows servers.
cards.why: FSx for Windows gives native SMB/Windows file system; EFS is NFS and not supported for Windows servers.

cards.scenario: Move Lambda app and Aurora MySQL to another org account, same Region, least downtime (select two).
cards.ok: Share Aurora cluster via AWS RAM and clone in target + re-create Lambda from ZIP in target S3.
cards.bad: Snapshot Aurora, share snapshot, restore in target account.
cards.why: Aurora clone via RAM is faster and more space-efficient than snapshot restore; Lambda functions cannot be shared via RAM.

cards.scenario: Assess hundreds of Hyper-V servers: processes, CPU/memory load, network dependencies (select three).
cards.ok: Deploy AWS Transform discovery tool, create migration assessment job, use results for right-sizing and waves.
cards.bad: Custom PowerShell inventory script uploaded to AWS Transform for assessment.
cards.why: The discovery tool collects process, utilization and dependency data; basic PowerShell inventory lacks utilization and dependencies.

cards.scenario: Warm-standby DR: secondary Region ASG at zero, cross-Region RDS replica; cost-effective failover, not active-active.
cards.ok: Route 53 failover record to secondary ALB; health check via SNS invokes Lambda to scale ASG, promote replica.
cards.bad: Weighted records (100 and 0) with health check, SNS and Lambda adjusting weights and promoting replica.
cards.why: Failover routing is built for active-passive switchover; weighted records need extra Lambda logic to shift traffic.

cards.scenario: Migrate on-premises VMs and SMB storage server to EC2, preserving software and configuration.
cards.ok: FSx for Windows via DataSync agent for SMB data; upload VM images to S3; VM Import/Export to EC2.
cards.bad: Export VMs as OVF to S3 and import with VM Import/Export; no storage server handling.
cards.why: VM Import/Export preserves server configuration; DataSync to FSx for Windows also moves the SMB share data.

cards.scenario: Rotate EC2 SSH keys after employee departure, fleet managed in Systems Manager.
cards.ok: New key pair, push public key to authorized_keys via Run Command AWS-RunShellScript.
cards.bad: New key pair, run shell script through Systems Manager Automation.
cards.why: authorized_keys needs the public key, pushed with Run Command; Automation runs runbooks.

cards.scenario: Restrict S3 data lake access to approved networks, no public internet (select three).
cards.ok: S3 access point + bucket policy on s3:DataAccessPointArn + Gateway VPC endpoint.
cards.bad: Bucket policy on s3:DataAccessPointAccount + NAT gateway routing.
cards.why: Access point ARN condition limits path; Gateway endpoint keeps traffic private. NAT gateway still uses internet.

cards.scenario: Prevent PROD OU accounts altering critical security groups' rules.
cards.ok: Tag critical security groups, SCP denies ec2:AuthorizeSecurityGroup* on that resource tag.
cards.bad: SCP denies ec2:AuthorizeSecurityGroup* when aws:SourceIp is 0.0.0.0/0.
cards.why: Tag-conditioned SCP protects specific groups; source-IP condition only targets open-CIDR rules.

cards.scenario: WorkSpaces reachable only from HQ and satellite offices; a new office is coming.
cards.ok: WorkSpaces directory with IP access control group rules listing the office CIDRs.
cards.bad: WorkSpaces with directory and AWS Direct Connect for secure access from offices.
cards.why: IP access control groups restrict by source CIDR; a new office is one rule. Direct Connect does not restrict clients.

cards.scenario: Each OU leader sees charge breakdown across their OU accounts; which tooling?
cards.ok: CUR from management account to QuickSight dashboard shared with leaders.
cards.bad: Systems Manager Explorer dashboard fed by per-member-account CURs.
cards.why: Management-account CUR covers the org; QuickSight dashboards share per leader.

cards.scenario: Each OU views detailed usage/cost breakdown for thousands of member accounts.
cards.ok: CUR in management account to central S3, visualized in QuickSight.
cards.bad: Lambda in management account creates a CUR inside each member account.
cards.why: CUR is the most comprehensive data source; QuickSight dashboards visualize it, not Trusted Advisor.

cards.scenario: Weekly CSV of Lambda memory use, recommended memory, savings; least development.
cards.ok: Compute Optimizer, EventBridge weekly Lambda calling ExportLambdaFunctionRecommendations.
cards.bad: Lambda Insights enabled, weekly Lambda compiles findings into CSV.
cards.why: Compute Optimizer already gives Lambda memory recommendations and savings; export API avoids building analysis.

cards.scenario: Central, cost-effective spend alerts and monthly report per department head.
cards.ok: Management-account AWS Budgets with member-account filters emailing department heads.
cards.bad: Budgets with SNS alerts configured separately inside each department account.
cards.why: One management-account Budgets with filters is centralized; per-account setups are not.

cards.scenario: Baseline EC2 use and right-size, no past usage patterns, cost-effective.
cards.ok: CloudWatch agent on instances, opt in to Compute Optimizer, wait about 12 hours.
cards.bad: Enterprise Support for Trusted Advisor extended checks and Incident Manager.
cards.why: Compute Optimizer needs opt-in and agent metrics, delivering recommendations within about 12 hours; no Enterprise Support.

cards.scenario: Collect and back up logs automatically from ASG instances about to be terminated.
cards.ok: ASG terminating lifecycle hook (default CONTINUE); EventBridge on Terminating:Wait invokes Lambda to SendCommand SSM Automation to S3.
cards.bad: SSM OpsCenter OpsItem runbook calls CompleteLifecycleAction with ABANDON to pause termination.
cards.why: A lifecycle hook holds the instance in Terminating:Wait so backup can run; ABANDON ends the action and terminates immediately.

cards.scenario: Teams patch with different tools; consolidated patch status across all servers (select two).
cards.ok: Register servers as Systems Manager managed nodes + use Patch Manager for operations and compliance reports.
cards.bad: Custom AWS Config rule with SSM Automation remediation, reports sent to S3.
cards.why: Patch Manager handles hybrid fleets and gives a built-in patch status view; Config custom rules rebuild that.

cards.scenario: Accounting must bill analytics division for tagged resources across accounts in an organization.
cards.ok: Activate cost allocation tag in management account; Cost and Usage Reports to S3; filter by tag.
cards.bad: Activate the cost allocation tag in the analytics division's own account; CUR with Athena.
cards.why: Cost allocation tags activate from the management account for org-wide, cross-account cost tracking; member accounts cannot.
